basic_info.item_name: KTH Formula Student (KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
basic_info.competition_series: FSG (Formula Student Germany) - primary driverless entries since 2019; also FSA (Formula Student Austria) and, as of 2026, FS Czech (Driverless)
basic_info.summary: KTH Formula Student was founded in 2003 (combustion 'R' series) and has produced electric cars since 2013 ('Re' series, then 'EV'/'DeV' series), giving the driverless program a mature EV base to build on. Driverless-specific engineering work (an ISO 26262-informed Emergency Brake System thesis, and a Perception & SLAM software project tagged 'KTHFSDV1718') began around 2017, timed to FSG's 2017 introduction of the Driverless class and its new 2018 EBS requirement. KTH entered its first FSG Driverless class competition in 2019 (car #471, 19th place, 199.19 points), converting a single electric car between EV and DV configurations rather than building a dedicated DV chassis. COVID-19 then stalled the program badly: the next car, DeV17, took roughly four years (2019-2023) to complete, and KTH's internal EECS news team described summer 2025 (DeV19) as the team's 'first ever driverless events' in a way that suggests years without a genuinely completed autonomous dynamic run despite having formally entered the DV class since 2019. Recent FSG Driverless placings (26th/65.00 pts in 2024, 35th/50.00 pts in 2025, 21st/88.30 pts at FS Czech in 2026) show a program that is present in the class but not yet consistently scoring at a high level.

history.ramp_phases: [uncertain] No explicitly named ramp phases were found in KTH's own public sources. Inferred: (1) EV platform build-up 2013-2017 ('Re'/'EV' series), (2) DV concept & safety-case work 2017-2018 (EBS thesis, Perception & SLAM prototype), (3) first DV competition entry 2019, (4) multi-year COVID-disrupted rebuild 2020-2023 (DeV17), (5) DeV18/DeV19 seasonal cadence resumes 2024-2025 with declining/mixed points, (6) 2026 - 20th car in development.
history.what_slipped: The clearest, best-evidenced slip is the ~4-year build window for DeV17 (2019-2023) versus KTH's normal roughly one-car-per-year cadence, consistent with COVID-19-era disruption common across FS teams in 2020-2021. A second, softer signal: KTH's own internal EECS news article (Oct 2025) frames summer 2025 as the team's 'first ever driverless events,' even though team results show a scored FSG Driverless entry back in 2019 (199.19 points) - implying that after the 2019 entry, the team went a substantial period without actually completing driverless dynamic events, only reliably doing so again around 2024-2025. Declining points from 199.19 (2019) to 65.00 (2024) and 50.00 (2025) also suggest reliability/consistency regressed relative to the original 2019 entry.
history.platform_prerequisites: Yes. KTH had already been building electric racecars since 2013 ('Re' series, then 'EV'/'DeV' series) before starting driverless-specific work around 2017 - roughly 4 years of EV-only development preceded the DV program. KTH also does not run a separate dedicated DV chassis: the team converts a single electric car between EV and DV configuration each season, which is itself a resource-driven design constraint on the DV program.

technical_features.ebs_design: Pneumatic Emergency Brake System retrofit onto the pre-existing hydraulic service-brake line: a CO2 gas cartridge pressurizes a pneumatic cylinder via a normally-open 3/2 EBS valve; the cylinder is coupled to an electric rotating actuator that pulls the brake pedal via a steel wire when triggered, mimicking manual braking. Two fully independent hydraulic circuits (front/rear) are retained downstream. A separate electric servo motor (service brake actuator) is used both for normal autonomous longitudinal braking control and as a redundant fallback if the pneumatic EBS fails - the system logic explicitly checks pneumatic tank pressure and hydraulic line pressure and latches a 'Failed_pneumatic_EBS' flag to hand off to the service-brake actuator. With a 1cm lever arm, the actuator design was sized to pull a mass equivalent of 84-110kg (approx. 840-1100N). Source: KTH Master's thesis SD221X (Markus Bölander, 2018), built around ISO 26262 functional safety and satisfying DT.3.2/DT.4-type shutdown/EBS requirements.
technical_features.ebs_development_duration: Approximately 6-9 months of formal thesis work (PDF metadata creation Dec 2017, thesis defended 27 June 2018) building on earlier informal concept work
technical_features.ebs_cost_estimate: [uncertain] Not disclosed numerically in accessible sources; the thesis notes the design was constrained by 'limited resources in terms of money and time'
technical_features.steering_actuation: [uncertain] A 2023 KTH bachelor's thesis ('Optimizing a Steering System for a KTH Formula Student Race car', Carl Elgcrona & Emil Nordahl) developed and bench-tested a PI-controller for the electromechanical steering actuator over CAN bus, evaluating message periodicity and priority effects. The controller met most requirements but fell short of the target 'more than 180 degrees of cumulative change in steering angle in one second,' and the authors recommend moving to Model Predictive Control (MPC) in future work. Specific actuator motor model, gearing, and DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism were not found in accessible sources.
technical_features.brake_actuation: Electric servo motor (also documented as the EBS redundancy actuator) used for normal-mode autonomous longitudinal braking/velocity control, separate from the pneumatic EBS used only for emergency stops.
technical_features.chassis_impact: [uncertain] Not found in accessible sources beyond the EBS/service-brake retrofit onto the existing brake line
technical_features.compute_platform: [uncertain] Specific onboard compute model (e.g. Jetson class vs. x86) was not confirmed in accessible sources; the team's public sensor-driver repositories (ZED, Ouster, Basler, SBG) imply a compute unit capable of running multiple ROS driver nodes plus a LiDAR-inertial odometry pipeline.
technical_features.sensor_suite: ZED stereo camera (via team's zed_ros_driver_pkg), Ouster LiDAR (ouster_ros_driver_pkg), Basler industrial camera (basler_ros_driver_pkg), and an SBG Systems IMU/INS (sbg_ros_driver) - all maintained as public ROS driver packages under the KTHFSDV GitHub organization. Cone color and depth are inferred from the camera pipeline per public descriptions of the perception system.
technical_features.shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] The 2018 EBS thesis discusses integration with the GLVMS/ASMS startup sequence and use of the Remote Emergency System (RES) to trigger EBS, but specific DS-relay/EBS-relay wiring per DT.4 was not confirmed in accessible excerpts.
technical_features.remote_stop_system: [uncertain] Referenced generically as a 'Remote Emergency System (RES)' in the 2018 EBS thesis; vendor/model not disclosed
technical_features.custom_pcbs: [uncertain] General team PCB sourcing is documented (NCAB Group supplies primarily 2-layer, 1oz copper, HASL-finish boards plus one 8-layer, up to 6oz-copper board for high-voltage applications), but this covers the whole electric powertrain, not DV-specific boards; no DV-specific custom PCB design/fab/bring-up duration was found.
technical_features.software_stack: ROS-based (Catkin-style packages, C++ and Python), split across sensor-driver nodes (ZED, Ouster, Basler, SBG), a LiDAR-inertial odometry node (direct_lidar_inertial_odometry, described by the team as 'a new lightweight LiDAR-inertial odometry algorithm with a novel coarse-to-fine approach'), a lidar_undistortion motion-correction package, an EKF state-estimation node fusing IMU, wheel speed, and GPS, and a torque_vectoring control package.
technical_features.ros_version: [uncertain] ROS1/Catkin, based on public repo structure (e.g. 'Catkin package' description for lidar_undistortion); no confirmation of a ROS2 migration was found
technical_features.perception_approach: ZED stereo camera plus Ouster LiDAR based cone detection; per public project descriptions, the pipeline infers cone color and calculates depth for each cone candidate, publishing detected cones in the camera frame before they are plotted on the SLAM map. Specific detector architecture (CNN/YOLO variant vs. classical) was not confirmed in accessible sources.
technical_features.slam_localization_approach: Extended Kalman Filter (per public repo roym899/kthfsdv-ekf) fusing IMU, speedometer/wheel-speed, and GPS measurements for state estimation, combined with a lightweight LiDAR-inertial odometry front end (direct_lidar_inertial_odometry) for motion estimation; cones are plotted to a map while the car simultaneously determines its global position via SLAM, per public project summaries.
technical_features.control_approach: PI-controller for steering (2023 bachelor thesis, bench-tested over CAN, found to fall short of a 180 deg/s cumulative steering-angle-change target; MPC recommended as future work); a torque_vectoring package exists in the team's public repos for longitudinal/lateral control allocation. Specific lap-control method (pure pursuit/Stanley/MPC) for the full autonomous stack was not confirmed.
technical_features.simulation_tooling: fssim - a Python, MIT-licensed Formula Student simulator maintained in the team's public GitHub organization for FSD competition development.
technical_features.open_source_repos: github.com/KTHFSDV (official org, ~8 repos): direct_lidar_inertial_odometry (LiDAR-inertial odometry), zed_ros_driver_pkg, ouster_ros_driver_pkg, basler_ros_driver_pkg, sbg_ros_driver (sensor drivers), lidar_undistortion (motion undistortion), fssim (simulator), torque_vectoring (control). Useful as a reference for sensor driver integration and simulation setup, though it does not expose a full perception/SLAM/planning stack publicly. Community/course repos add further insight: github.com/theoneandonlywoj/KTH-Formula-Student-Driverless (computer vision), github.com/javirasu/PerceptionAndSlam_KTHFSDV1718 (2017/2018 Perception & SLAM), github.com/roym899/kthfsdv-ekf (EKF sensor fusion).

milestone_significance.critical_path_items: 1) Maturing the electric powertrain/chassis platform first (2013-2017) before starting DV-specific work, since KTH runs a single car converted between EV and DV configuration rather than a dedicated DV chassis. 2) The EBS functional-safety case: the team's own 2018 thesis states there was 'currently no documentation' of ISO 26262-style functional safety applied to FS EBS design at the time, meaning KTH had to build the safety case largely from first principles rather than copying a reference design. 3) Recovering program continuity after COVID-19: the ~4-year gap to deliver DeV17 (2019-2023) and the multi-year gap to what KTH's own news team called the 'first ever driverless events' (2025) shows organizational/team-continuity risk was as large a gating factor as the technology itself.
milestone_significance.long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No numeric lead times (in weeks) were disclosed in accessible sources for LiDAR, camera, IMU/INS, or compute hardware.
milestone_significance.first_dynamic_test_date: [uncertain] Not found in accessible sources; inferred to be prior to the August 2019 FSG Driverless debut
milestone_significance.validation_strategy: For the EBS specifically, KTH applied an ISO 26262-based functional safety lifecycle (hazard analysis, safety goals, functional safety concept, DFMEA-style failure mode review) rather than ad hoc testing alone, per the 2018 EBS thesis. For steering, the 2023 bachelor thesis built dedicated CAN-bus bench-test infrastructure to characterize controller performance (message periodicity/priority effects) against a defined angular-velocity requirement before recommending further validation on the actual vehicle. No description of a whole-system validation strategy (e.g. required test-track hours before competition) was found.

competition_ecosystem.rules_compliance_challenges: The EBS requirement was brand new for the 2018 season (FSG introduced Driverless in 2017; EBS became mandatory for 2018), and KTH's own thesis explicitly notes there was no existing documentation or reference design for FS EBS functional safety at that time - the team had to interpret and satisfy the requirement without precedent. The steering system also had to meet a specific angular-velocity performance bar (cumulative >180 degrees of steering angle change in one second per the 2023 thesis's stated requirement), which the tested PI-controller did not fully achieve.

performance_metrics.dv_event_results: FSG 2019 Driverless: 19th place, 199.19 points (car #471). FSG 2024 Driverless: 26th place, 65.00 points. FSG 2025 Driverless: 35th place, 50.00 points. FS Czech 2026 Driverless: 21st place, 88.30 points. (Source: formulastudent.de team results page, team ID 919; no FSG Driverless results found in the database for 2020-2023, consistent with the COVID-era build gap.)
performance_metrics.autonomous_speeds_achieved: [uncertain] Not found in accessible sources; general vehicle top speed (electric, human-driven configuration) reported as 155 km/h with 0-100 km/h in 3.5s (Scania 2019 article) - not a driverless-mode figure
performance_metrics.ebs_deceleration_achieved: [uncertain] Not measured/reported in accessible sources; the 2018 thesis cites a rules-derived target of at least 8 m/s^2 average deceleration (velocity-time diagram example in the thesis), which is a specification reference rather than a confirmed achieved value
performance_metrics.reliability_notes: Points fell from 199.19 (2019 debut) to 65.00 (2024) and 50.00 (2025) before recovering to 88.30 at FS Czech 2026, suggesting inconsistent reliability across the COVID-disrupted rebuild years. The team's own Oct 2025 internal news framed that season as effectively a fresh start for driverless ('first ever driverless events'), and separately noted the electric car was 'one of only 40 teams to complete the endurance event' at FSG/FSA that summer (an EV-class achievement, cited here for program-health context).

top_mistakes: [uncertain] Not directly stated by the team in accessible sources. Inferred from the record: relying on a single car converted between EV and DV configuration each year likely limited how much dedicated DV testing time was available; the ~4-year gap to deliver DeV17 (2019-2023) suggests the program lacked resilience to a major disruption (COVID-19), losing multiple seasons of DV-specific iteration and, per the team's own framing, effectively restarting its driverless competition experience by 2025.
advice_for_new_teams: [uncertain] No direct quotes from KTH Formula Student were found in accessible sources.
team_structure_dv: KTH Formula Student runs a single combined team (not a large, separately-branded DV subteam) of roughly 80-100 students across mechanical, electrical, industrial, and vehicle engineering disciplines, who build one car per season and convert it between Electric (EV) and Driverless (DV) configurations. Named leadership found in accessible sources: Fredrik Danielsson, Project Manager for the 2019 season (a Scania-sponsored Master's thesis student); Robin Wikström, Project Manager (2020); Kim Strinnholm, Technical Head of Powertrain; Jordi Altayó, Technical Head of Electronics (both circa 2020-2021); Albin Eriksson, Team Captain 2025/2026.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] The official team site states new members are 'generally recruited during the autumn semester' on a one-year design-build-compete cycle, typical of Formula Student teams generally; no KTH-specific structured knowledge-transfer program (comparable to, e.g., a dedicated onboarding academy) was found in accessible sources.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] Not disclosed in accessible sources; the 2018 EBS thesis notes the design was constrained by 'limited resources in terms of money and time' but gives no figure.
recommended_sequence: Inferred from KTH's own build order: (1) establish a reliable electric powertrain/chassis platform first (KTH spent about 4 years, 2013-2017, on EV-only development before starting DV work); (2) treat the EBS functional-safety case as a first-class engineering deliverable gated by rules (KTH ran this as a dedicated ISO 26262-informed Master's thesis before its first DV entry); (3) build core perception (stereo camera + LiDAR) and state-estimation (EKF fusing IMU/wheel-speed/GPS) in parallel as a software track, validated in simulation (fssim) before committing scarce track time; (4) budget explicit organizational slack for turnover/disruption - KTH's multi-year setback after 2019 shows that a single bad season (or a pandemic) can erase several years of DV competition experience if the team has no dedicated redundancy in staffing or car availability.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: KTH's actual time from starting driverless-specific engineering (late 2017) to its first scored FSG Driverless entry (August 2019) was roughly 18-20 months - inside a 24-month window, and achieved despite having to invent an EBS safety case with 'no documentation' to reference. That is a directly encouraging data point for UMSAE's 24-month target. However, KTH's post-2019 history is a cautionary tale, not a template: converting a single car between EV and DV configurations each year, rather than committing dedicated DV resourcing, appears to have limited how much iteration the DV system got, and a multi-year disruption (2019-2023) erased most of the program's early competition experience, with the team's own internal news effectively describing 2025 as a restart. For a ~9-person, software-focused UMSAE team that already has a running EV (skipping KTH's multi-year EV-first prerequisite entirely), the actionable lessons are: (1) budget the EBS/functional-safety case as an early, dedicated milestone rather than an afterthought: KTH did this via a full academic-year thesis before its first DV season; (2) do not treat DV as a part-time addition to a single shared car if avoidable - protect dedicated DV testing/build time so a single disruptive year cannot erase multiple seasons of progress; (3) use simulation (as KTH did with fssim) to keep software iterating even when the physical car is shared with the EV program.
